BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: The next low pressure system will be moving into the area starting Sunday. On Sunday, precipitation chances will be limited to eastern Oregon before spreading into SW Idaho by Sunday evening.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Continued warm and dry Friday with record high temperatures possible.
- Windy conditions on Friday ahead of a cold front.
- Valley rain and mountain snow along a cold front Friday night into Saturday morning.
- Cooler and unsettled next week with snow levels lowering to valley floors by the end of the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A strong upper level ridge remains centered near the Continental Divide while a deep upper level low in the Gulf of Alaska approaches the coast. This will keep southerly flow in place today, with near-record warm temperatures and dry conditions. Skies will be partly to mostly sunny with passing high clouds. Winds slowly increase as the low begins to move onshore late Friday. Expect gusts 35-50 mph across open areas of southeast Oregon and far southwest Idaho, strongest in remote areas of southern/western Harney County Oregon. Elsewhere, expect gusts 20-40 mph.

A cold front will enter central Oregon Friday afternoon and move east across our area Friday night, bringing widespread precipitation along the front. This system will be quick- hitting and weaken as it moves inland, with precipitation ending from the west late Friday night through early Saturday morning. Rain amounts of 0.05-0.25 inch will be common across southeast Oregon and the lower elevations of southwest Idaho, with 0.20-0.50 inch across the mountains. Snow levels will be above 7000 feet initially and only fall to 5500-6500 feet behind the cold front, limiting accumulating snow to higher mountains. Winds will decrease behind the front to 5-15 mph on Saturday, except gusts 15-30 mph will persist in the Magic Valley. Highs Saturday will be 10-15 degrees cooler in most areas, but still several degrees above normal. An upper level ridge will begin building overhead on Saturday as the system moves east with partly to mostly sunny skies.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The next low pressure system will be moving into the area starting Sunday. On Sunday, precipitation chances will be limited to eastern Oregon before spreading into SW Idaho by Sunday evening. The trough will hold together enough for a 50-70% chance of light precipitation late Sunday through Tuesday. A cold front will slowly move through the area west-to- east, starting early Monday. Breezy prefrontal southwesterly surface winds will warm temperatures by a few degrees Sunday compared to Saturday, switching to cooler northwesterly flow Monday and Tuesday. Snow levels will fall from 5500-6500 feet Sunday night to 4000-6000 feet by Tuesday, lowest across eastern Oregon. A brief dry period is expected early Wednesday morning before the next system moves in. This deep upper-level low will move overhead from mid to late week, bringing colder air than previous systems. Uncertainty currently surrounds just how cool the temperature will get and the extent of the accompanying precipitation. Regardless, precipitation chances are currently forecast at 30-50% late Wednesday through Thursday, with temperatures favored to cool a few more degrees and snow levels around 3500-5000 feet.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: The forecast pattern becomes much more complicated by mid-week next week. A series of strong upper troughs is expected to push from the northern Pacific into the intermountain west during this period.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above normal temperatures and dry conditions will prevail through Friday, followed by more seasonable temperatures this weekend into next week.
- Chances for rain and snow showers across the high country this weekend, with a few showers possible over the eastern plains.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A ridge axis remains just to the west of our forecast area today, with weak flow aloft. Unsurprisingly, this has led to another day of above normal temperatures and sunny skies across the region. We should see highs reach the mid to upper 60s across the Denver metro and eastern plains.

The upper ridge should begin to weaken tonight into Friday, as a weak shortwave approaches. We'll still see above normal temperatures during the day, but increasing cloud cover should hold temperatures in the low to mid 60s.

There's still a surprising amount of uncertainty with this weekend's forecast, as a shortwave (or the remnants of a more organized cutoff low) pushes southeastward from the Pacific northwest into southern Colorado by Saturday night. This will usher in some cooler air (high temperatures near normal), along with a gradual increase in moisture. What remains to be seen is if we manage to get any organized precipitation in our forecast area. Across the mountains, sufficiently steep lapse rates would favor widely scattered rain and snow showers initially on Saturday, before transitioning to scattered light orographic snow showers Saturday night as the flow aloft turns to the west. Across the I-25 corridor, it looks like it will be challenging to saturate the column below 700mb given a lack of appreciable synoptic scale ascent/upslope flow. However, some moisture could stream into the eastern plains where guidance generally advertises some light (~0.1") rainfall totals through Sunday AM.

That system should quickly depart the region on Sunday, leading to a cool but quiet end to the weekend. Temperatures should again remain in the low 50s for most of the plains. A slight warming trend is likely for the start of next week as broad ridging develops over the central CONUS, leaving most of the state in a drier southwesterly flow aloft.

The forecast pattern becomes much more complicated by mid-week next week. A series of strong upper troughs is expected to push from the northern Pacific into the intermountain west during this period. The first of these waves looks to arrive sometime by Tuesday or Wednesday. At this time, the best chance of precipitation looks to be over our northern mountains, with decreasing chances off to the south and east. I will emphasize that this type of forecast pattern is volatile, meaning that forecast confidence is rather low. Readers are encouraged not to focus on single, deterministic model solutions for the next few days.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Thursday...Fast southwest flow aloft develops again ahead of the closed low aloft across Idaho and Nevada.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above average temperatures and dry conditions are expected to continue through the end of the work week.
- Chances of precipitation increase over the weekend for the mountains, but remain low for the plains.
-A more active pattern is expected into the middle of next week, with precipitation chances returning Wednesday into Thursday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Yet another mild and quiet day across SE Wyoming and the Nebraska Panhandle as a highly amplified longwave ridge is located over our area. With 500 mb geopotential height values exceeding the 90th percentile per NAEFS guidance and essentially no clouds noted on visible satellite imagery today (okay, maybe a few cirrus), high temperatures across the region are expected to soar 10 to 15 degrees above average for this time of year. With light and variable winds thanks to weak gradient flow as surface high pressure remains in place, today is another fantastic day to get outside and enjoy the unseasonably warm weather. Tonight will again feature tranquil and seasonably cool conditions under mostly clear skies and calm winds. There is the potential for some patchy fog development overnight into early tomorrow morning across mainly the Nebraska Panhandle, as high-resolution guidance has moderate (30-50%) probabilities of fog and surface RH values exceeding 95%. Would not be surprised to see some additional patchy fog along the North Platte River Valley into Goshen County, but confidence is too low to include in the grids at this time.

Any low stratus should quickly dissipate after sunrise, with another warm day in store for the region to end the work week. Can expect slightly cooler high temperatures tomorrow (though still above normal) as the upper-level ridge axis gradually shifts to our east ahead of our next system. Can expect a general trend of increasing mid and high-level clouds from west to east throughout the day as moisture aloft gets transported over the region under 500-300 mb SW flow. Another dry night is expected overnight Friday into Saturday morning, with temperatures dipping to around the freezing mark for most locations.

We begin somewhat of a transition into a more active pattern to start off the weekend. On Saturday, 500 mb geopotential height falls will overtake the region ahead of a shortwave trough that will skirt by to our south, bring us some cooler temperatures relative to much of this week. Temperatures will be around seasonal norms (average high for Cheyenne for November 14 is 48 degrees), can expect more cloud cover, though mainly dry conditions as the bulk of the forcing for ascent remains well to our south over Colorado. There is a slight (10-20%) chance that a few areas mainly along and south of the I-80 corridor see a few rain and/or snow showers Saturday evening into early Sunday morning, with the best chance being over the Sierra Madre and Snowy Mountains, although any totals will be light and negligible. Ensemble guidance has generally backed off QPF over the last few runs for locations such as Sidney and Cheyenne, so not expecting much of anything (~10% chance) if a stray shower does manage to slide north of the Colorado border.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Sunday...As a weak shortwave trough aloft moves overhead, scattered orographic showers will be possible early in the day across the Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges, with drier conditions in the afternoon in the wake of the shortwave trough passage. Slightly warmer than Saturday with the change in 700 mb temperatures.

Monday...The flow aloft backs to southwest, inducing surface lee troughing across our forecast area, and producing a continued warming trend as 700 mb temperatures rise to near 6 Celsius. Continued dry with limited low and mid level moisture.

Tuesday...Looks like a breezy to windy day as the flow aloft strengthens in advance of an approaching shortwave trough aloft from Utah and Arizona. Low and mid level moisture still looks too scant for any precipitation to reach the ground.

Wednesday...A progressive negatively tilted shortwave trough aloft will move across our counties, spreading chances for showers from west to east, with somewhat drier conditions by late afternoon in the wake of the shortwave trough aloft.

Thursday...Fast southwest flow aloft develops again ahead of the closed low aloft across Idaho and Nevada. Looks like enough synoptic and mesoscale lift and adequate moisture to produce showers spreading from west to east, until the late afternoon when subsidence behind the shortwave trough aloft will make it drier. 700 mb temperatures suggest temperatures will be somewhat similar when compared to Wednesday.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: A cooler and drier Sunday leads to a warmer Monday as ridging once again translates by as a stronger trough digs back upstream. The passage of this trough will brings another round of valley rain and mountain snow by mid week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry conditions and above normal temperatures hang around for one more day before cooler conditions are ushered in.
- Valley rain and mountain snow returns to the forecast this weekend favoring the southern mountains and adjacent foothills.
- After a quiet start to the week an active weather pattern set up for much of next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: This evening's H500 hand analysis map has a highly amplified ridge over the Rockies...extending through central Canada and across Hudson Bay. The ridge is being flanked by a large digging downstream trough over the East and a pair of upstream cyclones over the EPac approaching the coastline. The ridge will translate to the High Plains tomorrow and br further squeezed between the two troughs but it's influence and the southerly flow ahead of the upstream system will keep another mild day in place. Highs will generally be around 5 to 10 degrees above normal even with mid to high cloudiness drifting through.
COOLER, WETTER CHANGE HEADING INTO THE WEEKEND:

Water vapor shows a lead system being kicked toward the Baja this evening by a much stronger cyclone dropping out of the Gulf of AK. A weak AR associated with this southern system will allow the first influx of moisture to be pulled across the 4 Corners on southerly flow as early as tomorrow morning...though the bulk of it will be remain well to the South. This moisture will be more of a primer for a stronger push of moisture moving in tomorrow night. A moderate AR is associated with the northern cyclone which will be impinging upon the Sierras through much of tomorrow as it drops southward. As it drops across the southern flank of the upstream terrain IVT suggests we get a more robust push of moisture into our eastern and southern CWA by late tomorrow evening. Don't expect much in accumulating precipitation until this secondary moisture arrives though some high elevation orographics snow showers and sprinkles in the lower elevations could be possible by sunset. Luckily this system is not brining the highly anomalous moisture as the past few and even though it drops in negatively tilted...will be short lived. Though not overly cold much of the precipitation above 8500-9000 feet should locked in as snow. The persistent moist southerly flow will allow the southern San Juans to once again catch the best precipitation for the event. Other ranges will do better Saturday morning and early afternoon as the front passes through and the overall dynamics aloft are the strongest. Snow levels hover around 9K before fropa then drop to mountain bases by sunset as the storm is exiting. Storm totals of 4-10 inches are most likely over the southern San Juans above 9K with ensemble spot forecasts suggesting higher amounts near a foot in a few favored locations. A bigger challenge is forecasting possible impacts as much of the snow should melt as it hits the roadways during the daylight hours...leaving only a few hours of slushy/snowpacked roads near sunrise on Saturday and over the northern passes after sunset before the system exits. For now will continue to hold off on any winter highlights with other mountain locations only seeing a few inches at best. The liquid precipitation forecast across the lower elevation basins of the San Juan River remain in the quarter to half inch range as the highest probability outcome and hydrographs show only minimal responses at this point.

A cooler and drier Sunday leads to a warmer Monday as ridging once again translates by as a stronger trough digs back upstream. The passage of this trough will brings another round of valley rain and mountain snow by mid week. IVT forecasts suggest a more robust push of moisture and QPF amounts increase as a result. Unsettled conditions persist into the end of the week as low pressure looks to take over much of the West. Forecast confidence is very low at this time due to differences in the timing, strength, and track of this late week system.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Tuesday and onwards, model solutions continue to show a high degree of uncertainty.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Showers move into the area Friday Night through early Sunday. Expect accumulating snow over the mountains and rain showers over the plains.
- After a brief lull Sun-Mon, cooler and more active weather looks to set in the rest of next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Mild and dry conditions will persist across the area through the next 24 hours. Temperatures over the plains will reach into the mid- high 60s this afternoon, with high-50s in the valleys. Meanwhile, mostly clear skies and relatively light winds are expected across the region.

Tomorrow will be a few degrees cooler, thanks to increased cloud cover and a weak backdoor cool front this evening. Winds will also pick up a bit out east, with gusty east-southeast flow closer to the Kansas border. POPs start to increase over the San Juans later in the day, though as of now no precip is expected to move into our CWA until Friday Night.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A quick-moving system will move through the area right at the start of the weekend, beginning late Friday Night and lasting into early Sunday. An upper low will pass just south of us, moving in from the west, bringing precipitation chances to most of our CWA. Snow showers will start over the southwest mountains late Friday Night, with the heaviest accumulations falling into Saturday morning. Expected snowfall totals have come down slightly since yesterday, with the system having sped up from previous model runs. The San Juans can expected widespread 3-6 inches or so, though a few areas at the peaks may see slightly higher amounts. The lower slopes of the southwest mountains, along with the rest of our higher terrain, will generally see 2 inches or less, with some portions of the Sangres maybe seeing 4-6 at the peaks.

Snow levels look to remain above 8 kft, so the lower elevations will be seeing all rain from this one. Most of the eastern plains should see passing rain showers by the end of the day on Saturday, with the heaviest rainfall over our southeast counties thanks to the low passing overhead. Meanwhile, the system will also bring in some cooler air, with high temperatures falling into the 50s over most of the area, with 40s over some of the valleys and colder temps for the mountains.
The system departs our area on Sunday, leaving drier and cool conditions through Monday.

Tuesday and onwards, model solutions continue to show a high degree of uncertainty. A stronger upper low and associated trough will move through our area around the middle of next week, bringing more widespread chances for precipitation and cooler temperatures. Snow levels suggest the possibility for snow at lower elevations as well. However, the path, strength, and speed of the system still varies considerably between models and individual model runs. Some solutions take the system north or south of us by a considerable margin, while others move the low directly overhead. In general, we can expect the mid-late parts of next week to be colder and more active weather-wise, but beyond that the details are not yet clear in the data. Latest trends show the system lasting through at least Thursday, with another potential system in the works for next weekend.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: After a brief break Wednesday into Wednesday night, yet another storm system could impact the area by Thursday morning.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry conditions will give way to widespread valley rain and mountain snow late Friday into Saturday.

- Two more storms arrive next week with the first on Tuesday/Wednesday that looks very similar to the Saturday storm, and another towards the end of the week that has high-end scenario potential, but run-to-run consistency has been lacking.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A high-amplitude ridge has shifted east of Utah into Colorado this evening while upstream, a couple of storm systems are noted on water vapor satellite imagery. One is a closed low off the SoCal coast, while a second, larger, closed low is approaching the PacNW. The southern low will be coming onshore near the Cal/Baja coast by midday Friday. This system will gradually weaken as it becomes absorbed into the southerlies that will strengthen ahead of the second storm, which will continue to make its way onto the PacNW coast on Friday. The two storms will eventually phase into a negatively tilted trough which will then cross Utah Friday night through Saturday.

Given the increased southerly flow, some moisture will spread north into Utah on Friday ahead of the southern stream storm. As such, expect isolated to scattered showers to develop Friday afternoon into Friday evening. This will take place under a relatively mild airmass, with snow levels remaining mostly above 8500 ft during this timeframe. Precipitation will then become more widespread Friday night through Saturday morning ahead of and with a relatively fast-moving cold front. Snow levels will quickly fall to around 6-7 kft by around midday Saturday. However, precipitation will mostly wind down by late morning or midday Saturday behind the cold front, with the exception of the mountains, particularly those areas favored in northwesterly flow, which will maintain brief orographics into the afternoon. Additionally, with warm temperatures over the GSL, expect some showers to continue developing of the lake into the central Wasatch Front and adjacent mountains as well.

Most valleys are expected to see storm total precipitation amounts between 0.4-0.7 inches near the I-15 corridor and less elsewhere. Meanwhile, mountains are expected to see 0.6-1.2 inches with locally higher amounts in the upper Cottonwoods and near Brian Head. Snow amounts remain generally in the 4-8 inch range, mainly above 7500 feet, with higher amounts possible in the upper Cottonwoods, Tushars, and near Brian Head.

A transient ridge will cross the area late Saturday through Monday, bringing a break in the weather. However, the pattern remains progressive, with the next storm system looking to impact the area during the Monday night through Tuesday night timeframe. This will be another relatively fast-moving system which will also bring widespread precipitation to the area. However, it looks like this could be a colder system, which will result in lower snow levels, potentially down to at least 5000 feet.

After a brief break Wednesday into Wednesday night, yet another storm system could impact the area by Thursday morning. There is good agreement in the large-scale pattern regarding the existence of this late week storm, but with uncertainties in the timing and evolution. Latest global deterministics are leaning towards this storm being a broad closed low which will slowly move through the region through the weekend, bringing an extended period of precipitation to the forecast area.

2660.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: Avalanche conditions are generally safe. Avoid isolated pockets of wind-drifted snow above treeline. Expect danger to rise going into the weekend as new snowfall stacks up on Saturday.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ben Pritchett
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe for travel, with too little snow to produce an avalanche. At high elevations, steer around firm, drifted snow below ridges or in gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has yet to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. Except on the steepest, highest-elevation, north-facing slopes, the mountains are snow-free. Avalanches will be unlikely until a deeper, layered snowpack builds. Once winter does arrive, even a small amount of snow with enough wind can create unstable avalanche conditions. If you're traveling in the mountains during or after a storm, be wary of steep, wind-loaded features at upper elevations and watch out for terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information as more snow accumulates
hazard_discussion: Due to a warm and dry fall season, the mountains in our forecast zones remain mostly dry, with little to no snow on the ground. As you're waiting for winter to arrive and the mountain snowpack to stack up, here are a few things to consider:
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ben Pritchett
bottom_line: You can expect generally safe avalanche conditions. The few spots where you may be able to trigger a slab avalanche are where you find wind-drifted snow on slopes facing the north half of the compass above treeline. Look for small cornices above a slope, or stiffer, smooth snow surface to illustrate any steep spots to avoid.
